title: Robots Are Still at GPT-1, and the Real Signal Is Success Rate, Not Loss
dek: The Scaling Law signal for embodied intelligence has already appeared, but we're measuring the wrong metric: low loss doesn't mean low success rate, and fitting the 17 steps that never touch the object is meaningless.
why: Xu Mengdi, assistant professor at Tsinghua's Institute for Interdisciplinary Information Sciences, on data, world models and In-Context Learning for embodied intelligence. The middle-to-late section on the data flywheel and the loss trap is the most valuable part.
who: Founders, researchers and investors working on embodied intelligence, especially anyone currently agonizing over data collection routes, world models vs. VLA, and how to evaluate model progress.
skip: The opening rapid-fire Q&A and the Hengshui High School story can be skipped; go straight to the embodied startup and data section after the 44-minute mark.

points.h: Pretraining isn't everything — adaptation is what matters
points.body: Xu Mengdi's CMU best doctoral thesis is called Building Adaptable Generalist Robots, and its core claim is: pretraining is extremely useful, but you can't expect a robot to succeed 100% of the time on pretraining alone. The defining feature of the open world is that tasks keep changing — a home has 20 objects today, a week later it has 30 of different kinds, and people's preferences change too. So the robot has to be able to adapt to changes in its deployment environment and improve itself. She explored two paths: In-Context Learning and test-time training, the latter changing only 0.5% of the adapter parameters — but change too many and it forgets the pretrained knowledge.

points.h: Why adaptation only became important now
points.body: Humans generalize well for two reasons: extremely strong priors, and learning things very fast. The mainstream approach until now was to scale data and models so that multi-task and instruction-following abilities got stronger — essentially giving the model a strong enough prior first. But Xu Mengdi points out this doesn't mean adaptation is unimportant — it's just that people only recently realized it. And adaptation places demands on the base model: you don't want the robot's self-learning process in a real setting to be terrifying, like smashing a cup. So starting from pretraining is reasonable.

points.h: Low loss does not equal high success rate
points.body: This is the most counterintuitive technical judgment in the whole piece. There's a very tricky point in robotics: loss is not directly tied to success rate. Loss can be very low while the final success rate is not necessarily low — there will be a lot of oscillation. Her example: a task might take 20 steps in total, and the first 17 steps involve no contact with the object. Even if those 17 steps fit extremely well, if step 18, when contact actually happens, has a relatively large error, the task fails easily. This is an imbalance in the time sequence. So a Scaling Law that actually means something should be: as data gradually increases and the model gradually grows, success rate on unseen tasks gradually rises.

points.h: Robots are still at the GPT-1 moment
points.body: Today's mainstream embodied models are still ‘pretraining + fine-tuning on the target domain’, which can be compared to the GPT-1 stage of language models — GPT-1 itself also needed targeted post-training to solve the corresponding tasks. What Xu Mengdi really wants to achieve is the GPT-3 moment: giving the model task information through ICL, through prompting, without fine-tuning, telling the model what to do only through context. That way the weight of fine-tuning drops further, it's easier to scale to more scenarios and complete more tasks, and ordinary people can use it too.

points.h: The data flywheel is a chicken-and-egg problem
points.body: The hardest point is whether you can give the model a stable data flywheel. That requires putting the robot into an end-user home or service scenario, having a suitable mentor to teach it, and the robot must show obvious progress after being taught for half an hour — only then will end users be willing to use it, and only then can the data flywheel start turning. But there's a chicken-and-egg problem here: the base model needs to be good enough and learn fast enough, yet the model also needs to get into the scenario first so users start using it, in order to draw out that base capability. So whether the data flywheel can be made to work is the riskiest point of all.

points.h: Data is defined by working backward from model capability
points.body: Data itself gets fed to the model, but the definition of data isn't conjured out of thin air — it's defined by the model's capabilities. When people define data, what they're actually doing is: figuring out what capabilities the model needs, and working backward to how the data should be collected. If you need smoother motion, the data has to be of the smooth kind; if you need fail-recovery ability, the data has to be collected with failures and corrections in it. And right now people's definition of model capability is still fairly vague, so the data requirements are vague too.

points.h: Each of the four data types has its own place
points.body: Xu Mengdi's position is that of a fusionist, because different data teaches the model different things. Teleoperation data is closest to the robot body itself, suited to the post-training stage, making the model more directly relevant to the target domain. Simulation data easily produces position generalization and texture generalization, making the model more robust to visual changes, suited to pretraining or the front end of mid-training. UMI data sits in the middle, more like robot data but cheaper to collect. Human data is the cheapest, can be spread widely across different scenarios, and what it teaches is scenario variation and task-relevant information, less tied to the specific shape of the morphology.

points.h: AI-written papers are obvious at a glance
points.body: Robotics papers have recently been doubling in number, and Xu Mengdi's way of coping is to scroll through articles promoted by the researchers she follows, because the author list itself has already done a layer of filtering. She can clearly see that some articles have a very large AI-written component. Her judgment: AI-written articles may pass review and actually get into some conferences, but overall the quality still won't be higher than human-written ones, because they look familiar but in fact many arguments are full of holes and there isn't much content. Once she discovers an article is AI-written, her interest in it is discounted.

terms.def: Adapting a model to a new task through context in the prompt only, without changing model parameters.
A model that maps vision and language instructions directly to robot actions.
A data collection method sitting between robot data and human data, with lower cost.
Model-agnostic meta-learning: letting a model learn to quickly adapt to unseen tasks — the occasion that got Xu Mengdi into the field.
A DeepMind work arguing that model parameters are equivalent to an RL algorithm.
Once you make a choice, you have to accept its weaker aspects.
